articles.title: Caltech’s tiny new chip can steer light in 74 quadrillionths of a second
articles.summary: A new Caltech device can redirect a beam of light in just 74 femtoseconds using another beam and a nanoscale silicon metasurface. The breakthrough could pave the way for dramatically faster photonic communications, computing, and sensing technologies.
articles.content:
Light can transmit huge amounts of information at extraordinary speed, which is why photonic technologies are being explored for faster communications, more powerful computing, and highly sensitive sensors. To make those systems work, however, researchers need precise ways to control the direction of light and change it extremely quickly.

Caltech researchers have now developed a device that uses one beam of light to redirect another in just 74 femtoseconds (74 quadrillionths of a second). That is roughly the amount of time light needs to travel across the width of a human hair.

"Steering light with light is very challenging because light typically interacts very weakly with matter. Using optical meta-surfaces (ultrathin carefully nanoengineered sheets), we can up the interaction strength to make this possible with much higher efficiency," says Harry Atwater, the Howard Hughes Professor of Applied Physics and Materials Science and the Otis Booth Leadership Chair of the Division of Engineering and Applied Science at Caltech.

The researchers report their findings in a paper recently published in Nature Nanotechnology. Lead author Claudio Hail carried out the research while he was a postdoctoral scholar in Atwater's Caltech lab. He is now an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at UC Berkeley.

Why Conventional Light Steering Has a Speed Limit

Many existing technologies for steering or modulating light depend on changing the electronic properties of a material. Examples include liquid-crystal panels used in projectors and optical chips found in telecommunications systems.

In these devices, electrons are pushed into higher energy states before returning to lower ones and releasing their excess energy. That relaxation takes time, creating a bottleneck that usually limits light modulation to nanosecond or picosecond timescales (trillionths of a second).

Atwater's team took a different approach by eliminating the need for an electrical signal. Instead, the researchers used a powerful beam of light, known as the pump, with a carefully designed pattern that temporarily altered the optical behavior of a material.

A second, weaker beam, called the probe, then passed through that material. Its direction changed according to the pattern created by the pump beam.

Using the Optical Kerr Effect

The system relies on a phenomenon known as the optical Kerr effect. When an intense beam of light passes through a material, it can briefly produce a very small change in the material's refractive index, which describes how much light slows down and bends as it travels through that material.

The effect comes from changes in the motion of electrons within their orbitals, regions around an atom's nucleus where electrons have a high probability of being located. Crucially, the electrons are not pushed into separate, longer-lasting excited states.

As a result, the change can appear and vanish almost as quickly as the light pulse itself. There is no need to wait for excited electrons to fall back to lower energy levels.

On its own, though, the optical Kerr effect is too weak to redirect a beam of light by an amount that would be useful in practical devices.

Nanoscale Silicon Pillars Amplify the Effect

To strengthen the response, the researchers created a meta-surface from a thin film of amorphous silicon. The surface was covered with nanoscale pillars, each smaller than the wavelength of the pump's light.

By carefully choosing the size and spacing of these pillars, the team caused light to remain inside the meta-surface slightly longer and circulate within it instead of simply passing straight through.

That additional interaction time amplified the small refractive index change in the silicon. The resulting effect became strong enough to redirect the probe beam.

Using this design, the researchers steered light by angles of up to 13 degrees in as little as 74 femtoseconds. They also showed that the modulation speed was limited by the duration of the pump pulse (which was also 74 femtoseconds).

Even Faster Light Control May Be Possible

The researchers say the current speed limit comes from the laser pulses used to operate the system, not from the fundamental properties of the meta-material itself.

That leaves open the possibility of making the process even faster. With further development, the technology could reach timescales relevant to emerging photonic concepts including time crystals and synthetic time-varying optical materials.

The paper is titled "Ultrafast, reconfigurable all-optical beam steering and spatial light modulation." Along with Hail and Atwater, Lior Michaeli is also an author of the paper. He completed the work as a postdoctoral scholar at Caltech and is now an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at Tel Aviv University.

The work was supported by funding from the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and its Meta-Imaging Multidisciplinary University Research Initiative, the Swiss National Science Foundation, the Fulbright Fellowship program, and the Breakthrough Foundation. The Kavli Nanoscience Institute at Caltech provided infrastructure and support for the work.

This advancement has broad implications for future technology development and practical applications, with detailed context and explanation provided.

articles.title: Scientists are about to test Einstein’s gravity with exotic matter
articles.summary: Scientists have found a new way to create a controlled beam of muonium, an exotic atom containing a heavier cousin of the electron. The advance could allow researchers to test for the first time whether gravity acts on second-generation particles exactly as Einstein’s theory predicts. Any unexpected difference would be a major surprise and could potentially point toward new physics, including a hypothetical fifth force.
articles.content:
Does gravity affect every type of particle in exactly the same way? Researchers at ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen are preparing an experiment that could test that fundamental assumption using one of nature's more unusual particles.

"We have taken an important step towards carrying out an exciting experiment on this topic," says the professor of physics: "We want to measure the gravitational interaction of the muon."

The familiar matter that makes up people, planets, and nearly everything around us consists of protons, neutrons, and electrons. Physicists classify these particles as belonging to the first generation of matter. Two additional generations also exist, made up of heavier particles. One of them is the muon, a heavier relative of the electron that belongs to the second generation.

Researchers at PSI can create muons and their antiparticles using a large particle accelerator. When a positively charged antimuon combines with a negatively charged electron, the pair forms a neutral atom known as muonium.

Why Physicists Want to Test Muons

The Standard Model of particle physics describes these different generations of particles, but it does not explain why nature has multiple generations in the first place.

"But we physicists do not yet understand why these additional generations exist at all in the first place," says Soter. "And why are there three in total?"

That mystery raises another important question. Do the heavier particles of the second and third generations respond to gravity in exactly the same way as the lighter particles found in the first generation?

Testing Einstein's Equivalence Principle

For ordinary matter, objects at the same location in a gravitational field fall at the same rate. Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton recognized this universality of free fall centuries ago. It later became central to Albert Einstein's theory of gravity through the equivalence principle, which connects gravitational mass with inertial mass.

So far, however, researchers have demonstrated this principle only with ordinary matter or first-generation antimatter. Measuring how muonium behaves under gravity would provide the first test involving a second-generation particle.

"The exotic muonium is very well suited to this because it is a neutral atom," explains Soter: "After all, to make something fall, you need something neutral."

Neutrality is essential because gravity is extremely weak compared with electromagnetism. If researchers tried to perform the experiment with a charged particle, stray electromagnetic fields could overwhelm the gravitational effect they are attempting to detect.

Muonium presents another major obstacle. Muons survive for only about 2.2 microseconds before decaying. Earlier methods also produced muonium atoms traveling at different speeds and in many directions, making them poorly suited for extremely precise gravity measurements.

Researchers at PSI have now found a way around that problem.

"We have managed to produce the muonium atoms in a 'cold' state, which is what makes the gravity experiment possible in the first place," says Soter. "In this case, 'cold' means that the atoms propagate at similar speeds, almost parallel to one another."

Superfluid Helium Creates a Controlled Muonium Beam

The team describes its new method for producing muonium in Nature Physics.

"In order to achieve this, we used superfluid helium that had been cooled close to absolute zero at minus 273 degrees Celsius," explains Jesse Zhang, lead author of the study. "Superfluid helium is what is known as a quantum fluid, in which the individual helium atoms lose their identity, and which does not tolerate any impurities within it."

The process begins by directing antimuons from PSI's accelerator into a thin layer of superfluid helium. Inside the helium, the particles slow down. When an antimuon encounters a free electron, the two form a muonium atom with positive chemical potential.

That chemical potential effectively drives the newly formed atom out of the liquid. When it reaches the surface, the chemical potential is converted into kinetic energy, giving the muonium atom a boost that sends it vertically upward.

"So we're using the chemical potential as an atomic cannon," explains Zhang.

The muonium atoms must pass through the quantum liquid without collisions and at a predictable speed. Their lifetime is so short that any significant delay would prevent them from reaching the surface before they decay.

"For our experiments, we also rely on PSI's particle accelerator, which generates the world's most intense, continuous muon beams," says Soter. "Thanks to this high-quality source, a great many muonium atoms can be produced."

Watching Gravity Shift an Atomic Pattern

The researchers are now building an instrument known as an interferometer to measure how Earth's gravity affects the muonium beam.

The device takes advantage of the wave properties of atoms to produce an interference pattern. Earth's gravitational pull should cause an extremely small shift in that pattern. Measuring the displacement would allow the researchers to determine how gravity acts on the muon.

"We hope to be able to test the method for the first time with the atomic beam this year, and if all goes well, the actual gravity experiment should follow in two or three years' time," as Soter relates.

The new beam could also make much more precise laser spectroscopy experiments with muonium possible. Those measurements could improve scientists' understanding of the muon's mass and fundamental physical constants, another long-term goal of the research group.

Could the Experiment Reveal a Fifth Force?

If muonium responds to gravity differently from ordinary matter, the implications could be profound.

"That would indeed be surprising, and, in addition to other theories, it could point to the existence of a fifth force," as Soter outlines.

Modern physics recognizes four fundamental interactions: gravity, electromagnetism, the strong interaction, and the weak interaction. Scientists have repeatedly proposed the possibility of an additional fifth force, but no such force has ever been confirmed.

Discovering one is not the main objective of Soter's experiment. The immediate goal is more fundamental: determining whether one of Einstein's central principles also holds for a different generation of particles.

"I am completely open-minded," she says. "I simply want to measure, for the first time, whether the equivalence between gravitational and inertial mass also applies to the second generation of particles -- this alone is quite an inspiring piece of work."

This research is supported by the National Centre of Competence in Research Muoniverse.

articles.title: AI cracked the Navier–Stokes challenge. What does that mean for physics?
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02922-6Physicists and mathematicians are going beyond the classic equations of fluid dynamics to understand turbulence — often with the help of AI.
articles.content:
Chaotic vortices the wake of an aeroplane can contribute to aerodynamic drag.Credit: Photo12/UIG/Getty

Last week, OpenAI stunned the world by claiming that its most advanced artificial-intelligence model had solved a Millennium Prize Problem: one of just a handful of notoriously tricky mathematical conundrums that each come with a US$1-million prize. The AI solution proved mathematically that there are instances in which the Navier–Stokes equations — famous, nineteenth-century formulae that model how fluids flow — produce a ‘singularity’, predicting physically impossible infinite speeds for gases or liquids.

The news has opened up discussions about the blossoming mathematical abilities of AI, whether AI models are soaking up the unpublished work being done by others, who deserves credit and more. But there’s another question, too: what does this mean for the study of fluid flow?

The solution posted by OpenAI, which is based in San Francisco, California, explores a situation in which a vortex of fluid stretches out, becoming very long and very thin. George Karniadakis, an applied mathematician at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, has calculated that for air, the singularity appears when this vortex becomes around 70 nanometres wide — so thin that its width spans the typical distance that one air molecule travels before hitting another one.

It makes sense that this is the point at which the equations break down, Karniadakis says. The Navier–Stokes equations make a simplifying assumption that a fluid is a continuous substance, rather than a collection of chaotic molecules. When there are only a couple of molecules across the sample, that assumption is no longer a good approximation of reality, and the equations fail.

Limited scope

The Navier–Stokes equations were already known to be insufficient to model reality under certain circumstances. The Millennium Problem focused on fluids that are incompressible, which is a very good description of liquids such as water. For compressible fluids, researchers already knew that the corresponding version of the equations could give rise to singularities, says Charles Fefferman, a Fields Medal-winning mathematician at Princeton University in New Jersey.

The equations also don’t work for rarefied gases, so they don’t describe well, for example, what happens when a spacecraft re-enters the upper atmosphere, or when tiny amounts of fluid flow through microscopic channels.

One alternative approach is to use the Boltzmann equation, which treats a gas as a collection of individual molecules and models their behaviour statistically, rather than treating a fluid as a continuous substance as the Navier–Stokes equations do. Yu Deng, a mathematician at the University of Chicago in Illinois who won a Fields Medal this year for his work on the Boltzmann equation, told Nature in July that it is unclear what a breakdown of Navier–Stokes could mean for the Boltzmann equation. In principle, those equations could also break down in specific circumstances, too, he said. “Our understanding is very limited.”

Another possibility for modelling fluids is rigorous computer simulation of the behaviour of individual molecules. But this is computationally expensive and becomes untenable beyond the microscopic scale. In 2024, for example, researchers used a supercomputer to simulate a record-breaking 155 billion water molecules — which would generally fit into a cube just micrometres in size.

Some researchers tackle this computational difficulty by slicing up a problem into sections, using molecular dynamics to model very small scales, the Navier–Stokes equations to model large scales and an intermediate set of equations that lump molecules together to average their behaviour. Karniadakis calls this the ‘triple decker’ approach.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough where AI solved a longstanding Millennium Prize Problem related to the Navier–Stokes equations, advancing the understanding of fluid dynamics and turbulence. This achievement has broad implications for physics and engineering, representing a major technological and scientific advancement with potential wide-ranging benefits.

articles.personality_title_fr: L’IA résout une énigme vieille d’un siècle sur l’écoulement des fluides
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les équations de Navier–Stokes sont des formules mathématiques célèbres créées au XIXe siècle pour décrire comment les fluides comme l’eau et l’air se déplacent. Pendant longtemps, les scientifiques ont eu du mal à comprendre pleinement ces équations car elles prédisent parfois des résultats impossibles, comme des vitesses infinies dans les fluides.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Récemment, OpenAI a annoncé que son modèle d’intelligence artificielle (IA) avancé avait résolu un problème mathématique très difficile appelé Problème du Prix du Millénaire. Ce problème demandait si les équations de Navier–Stokes pouvaient créer une « singularité », c’est-à-dire un point où les équations ne fonctionnent plus et donnent des réponses irréalistes. L’IA a montré que ces singularités peuvent se produire quand un vortex de fluide devient extrêmement fin — environ 70 nanomètres de large, plus petit que la distance qu’un molécule d’air parcourt avant d’en heurter une autre.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle confirme où et pourquoi les équations de Navier–Stokes cessent de fonctionner. Elle aide les scientifiques à comprendre les limites de ces équations et montre la nécessité d’autres méthodes pour étudier les fluides à très petite échelle. Par exemple, quand les fluides sont aussi petits, les traiter comme des substances continues n’est plus exact. Cette compréhension améliorera les modèles utilisés en physique et en ingénierie, comme pour concevoir des avions ou étudier des gaz dans l’espace.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont explorer de meilleures façons de modéliser les fluides à très petite échelle, y compris en utilisant l’équation de Boltzmann qui considère les fluides comme un ensemble de molécules individuelles, ou en combinant différentes méthodes selon les échelles. L’IA pourrait aussi continuer à aider à résoudre des problèmes complexes en physique, accélérant les découvertes.

**Phrase clé** – L’IA a résolu un problème mathématique difficile sur l’écoulement des fluides, montrant précisément quand les équations classiques échouent et ouvrant la voie à de meilleurs modèles pour comprendre les fluides dans des situations extrêmes.
articles.personality_title_es: La IA resuelve un enigma de flujo de fluidos de hace un siglo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las ecuaciones de Navier–Stokes son fórmulas matemáticas famosas creadas en el siglo XIX para describir cómo se mueven fluidos como el agua y el aire. Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos han tenido dificultades para entender completamente estas ecuaciones porque a veces predicen resultados imposibles, como velocidades infinitas en los fluidos.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, OpenAI anunció que su modelo avanzado de inteligencia artificial (IA) resolvió un problema matemático muy difícil llamado Problema del Premio del Milenio. Este problema preguntaba si las ecuaciones de Navier–Stokes podían crear una 'singularidad', es decir, un punto donde las ecuaciones fallan y dan respuestas poco realistas. La IA mostró que estas singularidades pueden ocurrir cuando un vórtice de fluido se vuelve extremadamente delgado—alrededor de 70 nanómetros de ancho, más pequeño que la distancia que una molécula de aire recorre antes de chocar con otra.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque confirma dónde y por qué las ecuaciones de Navier–Stokes dejan de funcionar. Ayuda a los científicos a entender los límites de estas ecuaciones y muestra la necesidad de otros métodos para estudiar fluidos a escalas muy pequeñas. Por ejemplo, cuando los fluidos son tan pequeños, tratarlos como sustancias continuas ya no es preciso. Esta información mejorará los modelos usados en física e ingeniería, como diseñar aviones o estudiar gases en el espacio.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores explorarán mejores maneras de modelar fluidos a escalas muy pequeñas, incluyendo usar la ecuación de Boltzmann que ve a los fluidos como muchas moléculas individuales o combinar diferentes métodos según el tamaño. La IA también podría seguir ayudando a resolver problemas complejos en física y acelerar descubrimientos.

**Frase clave** – La IA ha resuelto un difícil problema matemático sobre el flujo de fluidos, mostrando exactamente cuándo fallan las ecuaciones clásicas y señalando el camino hacia mejores modelos para entender fluidos en situaciones extremas.

articles.title: How research funding took me out of the lab and into leadership
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02184-2Landing two large grants caused Anna Sandak to take on a managerial role in her team and made her reflect on what it means to contribute to research.
articles.content:
Many academics experience a point at which they transition from laboratory work to management, which can be an opportunity to foster growth in the next generation of scientists.Credit: Monty Rakusen/Getty

In April 2021, after six months of intensive writing, revising and reshaping of an idea that I had been refining for years, I submitted a research proposal for my first grant from the European Research Council — a part of the Horizon Europe funding scheme that focuses on researcher-led science. After waiting anxiously for another six months, I finally received an invitation to interview. I knew, therefore, that my proposal had been well received and would be eligible for resubmission should I ultimately miss out. So, after my interview in January 2022, I began to prepare for failure: I rewrote my entire proposal for resubmission.

To try to put the proposal outcome out of my mind, I turned off my message notifications, shut my e-mails and stopped checking my phone. The resubmission needed my full attention. It was only when my institute director called me in March that year that I broke my focus. I had won the grant. I’d been thinking of this achievement as the peak of my career, so much so that I had forgotten to imagine what my work would look like should I win — but I had no clue how much my job was about to change.

It was clear that the nearly €2 million (US$2.3 million) in funding, awarded over five years, would immediately transform my research group’s work. With this support, we could develop a new generation of living coatings for buildings: fungal-biofilm-based materials capable of self-repair and protection against ultraviolet light. What I did not expect was how quickly it would transform my job at the InnoRenew Centre of Excellence in Izola, Slovenia. Like many researchers, I spent years learning how to design experiments, analyse data, write papers and compete for funding. Academic training taught me how to become a scientist. But it had not prepared me to lead a growing team, manage people, navigate institutional structures and make decisions that affect the careers of colleagues and friends.

New peer-review trial lets grant applicants evaluate each other’s proposals

The questions that I was used to thinking about before receiving the grant — scientific considerations such as how to quantify the bioremediation capacity of fungal biofilm — quickly became ones such as ‘Where are our skill gaps, and who can fill them?’’. Hiring a researcher is not just about selecting the strongest candidate: every appointment shapes the expertise, culture and future direction of the laboratory. Decisions about collaborations, funding allocation and project priorities have similar consequences. They influence not only the science, but also the opportunities available to the people in the team.

I encountered a second gear shift two years later in 2024, when I secured a €3 million Pathfinder grant — a highly competitive funding scheme supported by the European Innovation Council, the European Union’s main body for funding cutting-edge research. This initiative seeks to develop emerging scientific technologies into marketable products and provides support in the form of a variety of business-acceleration services. Suddenly, our group’s ideas, which had existed mainly as carefully written grant proposals for other academics, had to be assessed not only for their scientific promise, but also for their technical feasibility, scalability, value and relevance beyond academia.

Strategic questions that had once felt removed became pressing: who would use this technology, what problem would it solve, how could it be produced and what partnerships would be needed to bring it into the world? As the European Research Council project grew, so did the team around it: researchers joined and the work began to open up questions that required expertise that wasn’t present at my own institute. My group, now made up of 16 scientists, found answers from researchers at six institutions across Slovenia, Austria, Slovakia and the Netherlands. Together, we formed a consortium, which I now lead.

Another way of doing science

Before winning my grants, my typical day was spent designing experiments, analysing results and writing manuscripts. Progress depended mostly on my own scientific decisions and productivity. Today, my work as a ‘researcher’ looks very different. The most obvious change is my distance from the lab. I used to spend my days immersed in experimental work, but now I usually only pass through in the morning to check that everything is progressing as planned. The rest of the day might involve revising papers and deliverables, preparing a project proposal, taking calls and attending meetings, interviewing candidates for a position, writing project reports for funding agencies and discussing continuing work with my consortium partners across Europe. I often end the day with budget approvals or meetings with university administrators.

It also illustrates the growth of a collaborative international research team and the transition of a scientist into leadership, which can inspire others in academia and research management.
articles.personality_title: From Lab Scientist to Team Leader: How Research Grants Changed a Scientist’s Career
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Anna Sandak, a scientist working at the InnoRenew Centre of Excellence in Slovenia, spent years focused on laboratory experiments and writing research papers. Like many researchers, she dreamed of securing major funding to support her ideas but had little experience in managing a large team or leading a big project.

**What happened** – In 2021, Anna applied for a large research grant from the European Research Council. After months of waiting and rewriting her proposal, she won nearly €2 million to develop living coatings made from fungal biofilms. This funding transformed her work, shifting her role from hands-on experiments to managing a growing team and making important decisions. Two years later, she won another €3 million grant from the European Innovation Council, which pushed her to think about turning her scientific ideas into real products and to lead a team of 16 scientists across six countries.

**Impact** – Anna’s story shows how winning major research grants can change a scientist’s career path, moving from doing experiments alone to leading a team and managing complex projects. The fungal biofilm coatings her team works on could protect buildings and repair themselves naturally, showing a new way science can help solve real-world problems. Her leadership also brings together experts from different countries, boosting teamwork and innovation.

**What’s next step** – With the new funding, Anna and her international team will continue developing their living coatings, focusing on making the technology practical and useful outside the lab. They will explore how to produce and sell these materials, build partnerships with businesses, and bring their scientific discoveries closer to everyday use.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Winning research grants helped Anna Sandak move from lab work to leading an international team developing innovative, sustainable building materials.
articles.personality_title_fr: De chercheuse en laboratoire à cheffe d’équipe : comment les financements ont transformé une carrière scientifique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Anna Sandak, scientifique au Centre d’excellence InnoRenew en Slovénie, passait ses journées à faire des expériences en laboratoire et à écrire des articles. Comme beaucoup de chercheurs, elle rêvait d’obtenir un financement important pour soutenir ses idées, mais elle n’avait pas d’expérience en gestion d’équipe ou de projet.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2021, Anna a soumis une demande de financement importante auprès du Conseil européen de la recherche. Après des mois d’attente et de réécriture, elle a obtenu près de 2 millions d’euros pour développer des revêtements vivants à base de biofilms fongiques. Ce financement a changé son travail, la faisant passer de la réalisation d’expériences à la gestion d’une équipe grandissante et à la prise de décisions importantes. Deux ans plus tard, elle a remporté une autre subvention de 3 millions d’euros du Conseil européen de l’innovation, qui l’a poussée à penser à transformer ses idées scientifiques en produits concrets et à diriger une équipe de 16 chercheurs dans six pays.

**Impact** – L’histoire d’Anna montre comment obtenir des financements majeurs peut faire évoluer la carrière d’un scientifique, passant du travail en laboratoire à la direction d’une équipe et à la gestion de projets complexes. Les revêtements à base de biofilms fongiques pourraient protéger les bâtiments et s’auto-réparer naturellement, offrant une nouvelle manière d’utiliser la science pour résoudre des problèmes réels. Son leadership favorise aussi la collaboration entre experts de différents pays, stimulant l’innovation.

**Prochaine étape** – Grâce aux financements, Anna et son équipe internationale vont continuer à développer leurs revêtements vivants, en se concentrant sur leur utilisation pratique. Ils vont chercher comment produire et commercialiser ces matériaux, créer des partenariats avec des entreprises et rapprocher leurs découvertes scientifiques du quotidien.

**En une phrase** – Obtenir des financements de recherche a permis à Anna Sandak de passer du laboratoire à la direction d’une équipe internationale développant des matériaux de construction innovants et durables.
articles.personality_title_es: De científica en laboratorio a líder de equipo: cómo las becas cambiaron la carrera de una investigadora
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Anna Sandak, investigadora en el Centro de Excelencia InnoRenew en Eslovenia, dedicaba sus días a hacer experimentos y escribir artículos científicos. Como muchos científicos, soñaba con obtener una gran financiación para sus ideas, pero no tenía experiencia en dirigir equipos o proyectos grandes.

**Qué pasó** – En 2021, Anna solicitó una importante beca del Consejo Europeo de Investigación. Tras meses de espera y de reescribir su propuesta, ganó casi 2 millones de euros para desarrollar recubrimientos vivos hechos de biofilms fúngicos. Este financiamiento cambió su trabajo, pasando de hacer experimentos a gestionar un equipo en crecimiento y tomar decisiones importantes. Dos años después, consiguió otra beca de 3 millones de euros del Consejo Europeo de Innovación, que la impulsó a pensar en convertir sus ideas científicas en productos reales y a liderar un equipo de 16 científicos en seis países.

**Impacto** – La historia de Anna muestra cómo obtener grandes becas puede cambiar la carrera de un científico, pasando de trabajar solo en el laboratorio a liderar equipos y proyectos complejos. Los recubrimientos de biofilm fúngico podrían proteger edificios y repararse solos, mostrando una nueva forma en que la ciencia puede ayudar a resolver problemas reales. Su liderazgo también une expertos de varios países, fomentando la colaboración y la innovación.

**Próximo paso** – Con esta financiación, Anna y su equipo internacional seguirán desarrollando sus recubrimientos vivos, enfocándose en hacer la tecnología práctica y útil fuera del laboratorio. Buscarán cómo producir y vender estos materiales, crear alianzas con empresas y acercar sus descubrimientos científicos a la vida diaria.

**Resumen en una frase** – Ganar becas de investigación ayudó a Anna Sandak a pasar de trabajar en el laboratorio a liderar un equipo internacional que desarrolla materiales de construcción innovadores y sostenibles.
